The Story of King Karakandu

I bow to Lord Jina, worshipped by the world, and I write the happy, pure story of King Karakandu.

He who first worshipped Lord Jina with just a single lotus and attained great fruit — his story, as written in other texts by ancient sages, I write in brief through their grace.

Neel and Mahaneel were kings of Terpur, the capital of Kuntal country. There lived a Jain-devoted merchant named Vasumitra. His wife was Vasumati. She had great love for dharma. In this merchant's household, there was a cowherd servant named Dhandatt.

One day, Dhandatt went to the forest to graze cows. In a pond, he saw a very beautiful lotus with about a thousand petals. He was captivated by it. So he jumped into the pond and plucked the lotus. At that time, the Naga princess said to him, 'Dhandatt, you have plucked my lotus, but keep this in mind — offer it to that great soul who is supreme in the world.' Following the Naga princess's words, Dhandatt took the lotus to his master and told him everything.

Vasumitra then went to the king and told him the whole story. No one could understand who was supreme in the world and to whom this lotus should be offered. After much discussion, they decided to ask the monks. They would know who is supreme in the world. With this decision, the king, merchant, cowherd, and many others went to the Sahasrakoot Jain temple. There, Suguapt Muni was staying. The king asked him, 'O ocean of compassion, O knower of the secrets of pure dharma, please tell us with kindness — who is supreme in the world, to whom this pure lotus should be offered?'

The monk replied, 'O King, Lord Jina, the lord of the entire world, free from faults like attachment and aversion, is supreme, for the world worships him.' Hearing this, everyone was greatly satisfied. What they sought had come easily. At that very moment, they all went before the Lord. Dhandatt the cowherd then bowed to the Lord and said, 'O you who are counted as supreme in the world, I offer you this lotus. Please accept it and fulfil my hope.' Saying this, the cowherd placed the lotus at the Lord's feet and departed.

There is no doubt that through this single act of worship with a lotus, Dhandatt attained great merit. He was reborn in heaven and eventually attained liberation. The king too, inspired by this event, became a devoted follower of Jain dharma and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that even the simplest act of worship, when done with pure intention and offered to the supreme recipient, yields infinite fruit. The cowherd Dhandatt, though uneducated and of low birth, through his sincere offering of a single lotus to Lord Jina, attained the highest spiritual goal. The wise should understand that devotion, not wealth or status, determines the fruit of worship.
